title: Beyond Kubernetes at Modal: How to Scale 1 Million Concurrent Sandboxes in Seconds
gist: Modal rebuilt its sandbox orchestration from scratch to abandon Kubernetes-style centralized coordination, reaching 1 million concurrent sandboxes and roughly 50,000 sandbox creations per second by making scheduling horizontal and workers self-authoritative, a design a AWS engineer calls the first credible signal that Kubernetes is not keeping pace with GenAI infrastructure needs.

themes.theme: Why Kubernetes hits scaling limits for AI sandboxes

insights.claim: Modal staff engineers Colin Weld and Connor Adams argue traditional container orchestration systems like Kubernetes struggle at million-sandbox scale because they rely heavily on centralized coordination and strongly consistent state.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Frames a structural argument that Kubernetes' core consistency model, not just tuning, is the ceiling for GenAI-scale ephemeral compute — relevant to any infra vendor evaluating build-vs-adopt-K8s decisions.
insights.locator: According to Weld and Adams, traditional container orchestration systems

insights.claim: In Kubernetes, load on both the scheduling algorithm and the central durable store (etcd) grows with the number of nodes and pods, and because both pods and nodes write to etcd multiple times, this creates serious issues under high pod creation rates or high pod churn since etcd is not natively shardable within a keyspace.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Identifies etcd's non-shardable keyspace as the specific bottleneck component; any vendor claiming Kubernetes-scale improvements should be evaluated against whether they've addressed this exact constraint.
insights.quote: which can create serious issues under high pod creation rates or high pod churn, and etcd is not natively shardable within a keyspace
insights.locator: In kubernetes' case, they explain, the load on both

insights.claim: Modal's engineers say overcoming Kubernetes' scaling limitations is feasible but requires 'serious work,' including rewriting or replacing etcd and parallelizing the scheduling algorithm — work substantial enough that Modal instead built a new architecture from scratch.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Suggests a fork-in-the-road for infra companies: invest in patching Kubernetes internals, or exit the ecosystem entirely as Modal did — a build decision with major engineering-cost implications.
insights.locator: They also note that overcoming this limitations is feasible

insights.claim: Modal's core design principle was that everything taking O(sandboxes) or O(nodes) load must be horizontally scalable by default, the sandbox creation path should be as simple as possible, and everything else should be secondary.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A reusable design heuristic for any team building high-scale ephemeral compute systems: optimize the hot path ruthlessly and treat all O(n) operations as first-class scaling risks.
insights.quote: To optimize for scale, we decided that everything taking O(sandboxes) or O(nodes) load must be horizontally scalable by default, the sandbox creation path should be as simple as possible, and everything else should be secondary.
insights.locator: To optimize for scale, we decided

insights.claim: Modal's fundamental architectural change was to stop coordinating globally and make scheduling behave like load balancing: each worker became its own source of truth instead of relying on a central datastore, and a fleet of parallel scheduling servers replaced a single serialized scheduler, contacting workers directly via RPC to request sandbox creation, with workers accepting or rejecting based on free resources.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: This decentralized, load-balancer-style scheduling pattern is a concrete architectural template other infra builders could adopt to escape central-coordinator bottlenecks.
insights.locator: The fundamental change Modal's engineers made

insights.claim: Modal's resulting architecture has only one remaining bottleneck: all workers publish their state as a single Redis stream, which load testing suggests remains viable until well over 100,000 workers.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Even a radically decentralized design retains one centralized dependency (Redis stream); this is the next scaling ceiling to watch as Modal grows past 100,000 workers.
insights.locator: The resulting architecture has only one bottleneck

insights.claim: In benchmarks, Modal created 1 million sandboxes in under a minute, with median startup-to-code time under 0.5 seconds.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A concrete, testable performance claim (sub-second median cold start at million-scale) that sets a new competitive bar for sandbox/serverless infra providers serving AI agent workloads.
insights.locator: In their benchmark, they created 1 million sandboxes

themes.theme: Industry reaction and implications for cloud infrastructure

insights.claim: Hopsworks CEO Jim Dowling commented on LinkedIn that 'new technical problems arise at every order of magnitude increase in scale,' suggesting Modal's team had to iterate its design multiple times to reach a reliable 50,000 sandbox creations per second.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: 50,000 sandbox creations/sec is the concrete throughput figure external observers are anchoring on as Modal's headline achievement.
insights.quote: new technical problems arise at every order of magnitude increase in scale
insights.locator: Commenting the announcement on LinkedIn, Hopsworks CEO Jim Dowling

insights.claim: AWS principal AI engineer Alex Jones said the key part of Modal's achievement was not trying to extend Kubernetes but 'walking around the whole thing,' calling it 'the first credible signal that Kubernetes isn't adapting fast enough to what GenAI infrastructure actually needs.'
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A credible outside voice (from a Kubernetes-adjacent hyperscaler) validating that Kubernetes may be structurally unsuited to GenAI infra — a signal worth monitoring for shifts in enterprise infra spend away from K8s-centric stacks for AI workloads specifically.
insights.quote: the first credible signal that Kubernetes isn't adapting fast enough to what GenAI infrastructure actually needs
insights.locator: More substantively, AWS principal AI engineer Alex Jones observed

insights.claim: Alex Jones predicts a decoupling of coordination from execution: the execution plane (like what Modal built) wants isolation boundaries appearing in milliseconds, while the coordination plane, where multi-agent workflows need shared memory and overlapping security boundaries, still wants what Kubernetes-shaped systems provide.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: A forward-looking architectural bifurcation thesis: future AI infra stacks may pair a fast, Modal-like execution layer with a Kubernetes-like coordination layer rather than one system doing both — a useful lens for evaluating infra vendors' roadmaps and partnership plays.
insights.quote: We're heading for a decoupling of coordination from execution. The execution plane wants what Modal built; isolation boundaries that appear in milliseconds. The coordination plane (where multi-agent workflows need shared memory and overlapping security boundaries) still wants what Kubernetes-shaped systems are good at.

insights.claim: Modal is a serverless compute platform built for AI workloads offering programmable access to CPUs, GPUs, containers, inference, training, batch jobs, and isolated sandboxes, and is not alone in pursuing highly scalable infrastructure with sub-10-millisecond cold starts to 'rebuild the cloud' — other projects with similar goals include Unikraft, Google Substrate, and Overdrive.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Names the direct competitive set (Unikraft, Google Substrate, Overdrive) pursuing sub-10ms cold-start 'rebuild the cloud' infrastructure — a watchlist for investors tracking the next-gen cloud compute category.
